The results of this exercise mirror the treatment effects: because radiologists do not correctly incorporate the AI’s information, the majority of patients are optimally decided either by the radiologist or the AI alone but not by the radiologist with access to AI.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s supervised-augmentation framing and materially extends it with experimental evidence that expert behavioral biases create a non-trivial delegation problem. Although based on radiology rather than legal practice, it strengthens the case for designing human–AI workflows around complementary expertise, oversight and institutional safeguards rather than assuming autonomous replacement.
qs: In addition to considerable legal and regulatory challenges that stand in the way of full automation, combining human expertise with AI input has potential gains that cannot be realized by exclusively relying on one or the other.

We add to this literature by developing an experi- mental approach that manipulates the information environment to compare behavior with a Bayesian benchmark, to document systematic biases, and to demonstrate that these biases result in a non-trivial delegation problem.6

st.t: Radiology assistance: Accuracy, teamwork and replacement diverge
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central distinction between standalone AI accuracy and effective human–AI collaboration, then materially develops it by identifying belief-updating errors and modelling selective delegation among unaided humans, assisted humans and full automation. Its findings support conditional rather than universal assistance, while not addressing broader workforce replacement or local demographic performance.
qs: Results show that providing (i) AI predictions does not improve performance on average, whereas (ii) contextual information does.

The results of this exercise mirror the treatment effects: because radiologists do not correctly incorporate the AI’s information, the majority of patients are optimally decided either by the radiologist or the AI alone but not by the radiologist with access to AI.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study materially strengthens the cluster’s case for selective, task-specific deployment: strong standalone AI accuracy did not translate into average gains from routine assistance, and outcomes varied with human and AI confidence. Its allocation model further shows that AI-only, human-only and assisted workflows should be chosen case by case, while cautioning that radiology findings may not generalise to generative legal AI.
qs: We find that AI assistance does not improve radiologists’ average diagnostic quality, even though its predictions are more accurate than 78% of them.
However, automating all cases is not necessarily optimal either because humans perform better than AI when the AI is uncertain.

st.t: Assisted performance: Gains vary by skill measure
st.an: The radiology experiment directly supports the cluster’s distinction between different performance measures: AI assistance increased agreement with AI without clearly improving accuracy against the diagnostic standard, and it did not uniformly reduce measured effort. This evidence weighs against treating convergence, accuracy and effort as interchangeable or inferring automatic substitution.

st.t: Human response: Stronger assistance can reduce effort
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified proposition by formally showing that human-only and combined-signal decisions can diverge and that their relative value depends on specified conditions. Its excerpts are proof fragments rather than empirical productivity evidence, so they reinforce the cluster’s emphasis on conditional joint performance without establishing a general advantage for either human-only or AI-assisted decisions.

kp.k: Experiment separates AI assistance from valuable human context
kp.d: The authors study radiology, not legal services, using 227 professional radiologists and 324 retrospective Stanford patient records. A two-by-two information experiment varies access to AI predictions and clinical history while always providing chest X-rays. Three designs combine within-participant comparisons, repeated assessments separated by at least two weeks, and assessments obtained without AI before providing AI. Main analyses cover cardiomediastinal abnormality and airspace opacity, with 41,920 patient-pathology assessments. The AI is the CheXpert image classifier, rather than generative AI.
qs: In total, 227 radiologists participated in our experiment.
We cross-randomize the availability of AI and clinical history, while the X-ray is always available.
The algorithm does not use any other patient information, such as the clinical history or vitals.

kp.k: Diagnostic performance measures expert consensus, not established ground truth
kp.d: The diagnostic standard aggregates probability assessments from five board-certified Mount Sinai radiologists with chest specialty, classifying a pathology as present when the average exceeds 0.5. The authors acknowledge that this is not necessarily actual disease presence: definitive tests may not exist, and follow-up outcomes are selectively observed. They argue that closer agreement with highly qualified expert consensus is valuable and report robustness checks using alternative standards. The document is a working paper, initially issued July 2023 and revised November 2025, not a peer-reviewed NBER publication.
qs: The diagnostic standard may differ from the “ground truth” presence of a pathology.
NBER working papers are circulated for discussion and comment purposes.

kp.k: Superior standalone AI does not ensure effective assistance
kp.d: Against the preferred diagnostic standard, AI achieves an AUROC of 0.85 and exceeds 78% of radiologists. A hypothetical statistical combination of human and AI signals achieves 0.88 and exceeds 86%, indicating potential complementary information rather than demonstrated collaborative performance. Experimentally providing AI does not significantly improve average diagnostic performance, even though radiologists move toward its predictions. The 78% comparison depends on the diagnostic standard; appendix comparisons using internal participant-derived standards place AI at the 43rd and 48th percentiles.
qs: In contrast, AI assistance does not significantly improve average performance.
Treatments where AI is provided reduce this baseline average deviation by 18.3%.

kp.k: Clinical history improves diagnosis without being available to AI
kp.d: Access to clinical history reduces deviation from the diagnostic standard by 4.0% of the control mean, with p < 0.05. This experimentally supports the value of contextual information held by humans but absent from the image-only classifier. The authors identify logistical and privacy obstacles to assembling such information for AI training. The finding establishes potential gains from incorporating human context, not proof that humans successfully combine that context with AI predictions.
qs: Access to contextual information improves performance on average.
We find that access to clinical history reduces the deviation from the diagnostic standard by 4.0% (p < 0.05) of the control mean.

kp.k: AI assistance helps or harms depending on uncertainty
kp.d: Average results conceal systematic heterogeneity. Assistance improves assessments and decisions when radiologists are uncertain, but harms them when radiologists are highly confident a pathology is absent. Confident AI predictions of absence improve human performance, whereas uncertain AI predictions in the middle probability range worsen it. Evidence is weaker for high predicted probabilities because relatively few cases fall there. The authors interpret harmful effects from additional information as inconsistent with Bayesian updating under correct beliefs.
qs: These findings reject a model in which radiologists are Bayesians with correct beliefs.
In the lowest bin of AI predictions, deviation from the diagnostic standard markedly decreases.

kp.k: Underweighting and dependence neglect explain failed information integration
kp.d: The preferred estimated model combines automation neglect—underweighting AI relative to one's own information—with signal dependence neglect—treating human and AI signals as conditionally independent despite their shared image information. Table 2 estimates the AI update coefficient b at 0.26 (standard error 0.02) and own-information coefficient d at 0.87 (0.01), using 11,420 observations. Model selection favors this specification over alternatives accounting for signal dependence; this modeling and testing exercise was not preregistered. The authors remain agnostic between non-Bayesian updating and Bayesian updating with an incorrect mental model.
qs: The second type of error is that radiologists exhibit automation neglect.
Our model estimation and testing procedure was not pre-registered.
In addition to over- and under-updating, such a decision-maker could also update in the wrong direction.

kp.k: Neglecting overlap can make additional information actively harmful
kp.d: The theoretical model distinguishes insufficient reliance on AI from failure to account for overlapping information. With correct dependence treatment and d = 1, automation neglect alone weakly improves expected decision quality when AI is provided; signal dependence neglect can instead induce updating in the wrong direction. The preferred model reproduces the observed deterioration under uncertain AI signals, whereas the Bayesian benchmark and the model featuring automation neglect alone do not. This is a mechanism inferred through model estimation, distinct from the randomized treatment effects themselves.
qs: Only the selected model, under which radiologists also neglect signal dependence, replicates the worsening of assessments with uncertain AI signals.
Thus, signal dependence neglect adds another dimension of potential mistakes in which the decision-maker does not correctly account for overlapping information of the AI.

kp.d: Radiologists spend an average of 2.79 minutes per patient. AI assistance slows them by approximately 4%, rather than delivering a productivity gain through faster reads; clinical history also increases time. Table C.6 estimates additional active time of 5.937 seconds for AI and 8.117 seconds for clinical history in the baseline specification. Timing analyses exclude design 3 because of learning effects. Thus, in this experiment, ineffective information integration is not offset by faster human work.
qs: On average, they spend 2.79 minutes per patient with large variability.
The results suggests that both AI and CH slow radiologists, but only by 4% in the case of AI (see appendix C.5).

kp.k: Selective delegation outperforms universal human oversight
kp.d: The authors estimate a delegation policy choosing AI alone, humans alone, or AI-assisted humans as a function of the AI prediction. It minimizes monetized decision loss plus human time costs, assuming zero marginal AI cost and $10 for either human modality. Their preferred policy generally automates cases with confident AI predictions and assigns uncertain cases to unassisted humans, rarely selecting joint assessment. For airspace opacity, almost all cases go to AI when the assumed false-negative cost is below $100; at sufficiently high costs, humans handle approximately 50% of cases, mostly without AI. These are modeled allocations, not outcomes of a deployed clinical system.
qs: However, automating all cases is not necessarily optimal either because humans perform better than AI when the AI is uncertain.
Only few cases are optimally delegated to radiologists with access to AI.
In other words, we find that radiologists should primarily work next to as opposed to with AI.

kp.k: Better integration could materially expand collaborative work
kp.d: The estimated airspace-opacity frontier permits lower decision loss alongside $5.0 in time-cost savings relative to unassisted human diagnosis at the minimum-loss frontier point. Under a counterfactual Bayesian decision-maker, human-AI collaboration grows markedly once false-negative costs exceed $100; even at $10,000, 21% of cases remain automated because AI and Bayesian decisions coincide. The authors therefore identify substantial unrealized gains from correct information integration, while treating effective training or experience as an open research question rather than a demonstrated remedy.
qs: By moving to the frontier point that minimizes decision loss, one can reduce decision loss while also saving $5.0 in time costs.

We also find that many more patients would be optimally diagnosed by a human with AI assistance if humans correctly combined AI predictions with their own information, thus pointing to the potential importance of learning or further training.

kp.k: Deployment conclusions remain conditional and domain-specific
kp.d: The experiment uses retrospective cases and structured reports rather than a live clinical trial. Delegation analysis treats pathologies separately and does not model strategic human responses, changing expectations about case difficulty, organizational incentives, or liability and regulation. The authors explicitly leave transfer to generative AI unresolved and distinguish substitution on individual diagnostic tasks from possible complementarity across the wider bundle of work. The source therefore provides cross-domain evidence about expert-AI information integration, not direct evidence of changes in legal staffing or services.
qs: For instance, our observation that humans optimally work next to as opposed to with AI may not necessarily hold for other cases such as generative AI.
The use of AI in practice will also be mediated by other organizational incentives and the regulatory environment.

Although we find that human radiologists and AI are substitutes on specific tasks (as defined by diagnosis of particular cases), they may still be complements in the overall production function which involves a bundle of different tasks (Acemoglu and Autor, 2011).

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Agarwal, Moehring, Rajpurkar and Salz find that superior standalone AI performance does not automatically translate into better AI-assisted radiologists; their delegation analysis favors assigning most cases to either humans alone or AI alone.
pts.d: The authors make these claims about radiology, not legal services. CheXpert outperformed 78% of participating radiologists by AUROC, but access to its predictions did not significantly improve average diagnostic performance. Assistance helped when the AI confidently predicted absence of a pathology, but harmed performance when AI predictions were uncertain; it also helped uncertain radiologists but harmed those highly confident that a pathology was absent. Clinical history, which the AI could not access, improved performance. The authors interpret the unrealized collaboration gains through an estimated model combining automation neglect (underweighting AI relative to one's own information) and signal dependence neglect (failing to account for overlapping information). Their economic analysis finds that selective delegation can reduce both diagnostic loss and human time costs, with few cases optimally assigned to AI-assisted humans. This is a modeled allocation result, not observed workforce replacement. Correctly combining signals would make human–AI collaboration valuable for many more cases.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence combines randomized information treatments, comparisons against an expert-consensus diagnostic standard, estimated belief-updating models, and an economic delegation exercise.
pts.d: The November 2025 revision of NBER Working Paper 31422 reports 227 professional radiologists assessing retrospective cases drawn from 324 Stanford patient records. Three experimental designs varied AI predictions and clinical history in a two-by-two information structure; the primary analysis covers airspace opacity and cardiomediastinal abnormality, with 41,920 patient–pathology assessments. The diagnostic standard aggregates five board-certified Mount Sinai chest specialists' assessments rather than independently verified disease outcomes. AI AUROC was 0.85; a fitted hypothetical combination of human and AI signals reached 0.88. Clinical history reduced deviation from the diagnostic standard by 4.0% of the control mean (p < 0.05). AI moved reports closer to its predictions without significantly improving average performance and increased reading time by approximately 4%. The selected updating model estimated an AI coefficient of 0.26 and an own-information coefficient of 0.87. Model estimation and testing were not preregistered, although the experiment was. Delegation gains derive from estimated diagnostic losses and assumed costs, not a trial of an implemented routing system. The source is a working paper identified as not peer-reviewed.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern a bounded retrospective experiment and conditional allocation calculations, not a dated forecast of professional displacement.
pts.d: The document was originally issued in July 2023 and revised in November 2025; the supplied text does not specify a calendar period for experimental data collection. The AI is an image-classification neural network, not generative AI, and lacks clinical history. The delegation model assumes zero marginal AI cost and a baseline human cost of $10 per case, routing on the AI signal while varying the dollar cost of a false negative. For airspace opacity, almost all cases are automated when that cost is below $100; at sufficiently high costs, observed human behavior implies human involvement in approximately half of cases, mostly without AI assistance. The analysis considers one pathology at a time and does not model strategic responses or changes in expectations under routing. Training, longer experience, organizational incentives and regulation could change the results, but their effects are left to future research. The authors explicitly leave transfer to generative AI unresolved. Hinton's 2016 five-year prediction appears as a quoted framing device, not the authors' forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate implications concern radiologists, healthcare organizations allocating diagnostic work, and patients; broader professional and employment implications remain conditional.
pts.d: Radiologists may retain value through contextual information and superior performance on cases where AI is uncertain, while some confident AI classifications could be automated under the model. Healthcare organizations face a choice among autonomous classification, unaided human judgment and AI-assisted human judgment rather than a presumption that assistance is always beneficial. Patients are the intended beneficiaries of reduced diagnostic loss, although actual patient outcomes were not measured. The participant pool included US-based and foreign radiologists, with approximately 14% US-based and about 60% reporting prior radiology-AI experience; all routinely diagnosed US patients. The authors suggest relevance to other expert classification tasks only insofar as similar updating biases occur. They distinguish substitution on particular diagnostic tasks from possible complementarity across the wider bundle of professional work, and provide no quantified employment or wage forecast.
